newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Siberia power cuts didn't affect diamonds - gem firm.
newsitem.headline: Siberia power cuts didn't affect diamonds - gem firm.

text.p: A senior official at Russia's largest diamond producer said on Monday that Siberian power cuts had not affected mining in the area and that the mine's management had reached a new accord with power workers.

"There was no noticeable fall in production of diamonds. It did not effect production," Sergei Lukishin, head engineer of Almazy Rossii-Sakha (ARS, or Diamonds of Russia), said by telephone from the Siberian production center Mirny.
ARS, Russia's largest diamond producer and sole authorised exporter, is negotiating a three-year export deal with De Beers Consolidated Mines Ltd.
"The situation was serious, but only in terms of negotiations," Lukishin said. "Everything was worked out through negotiation... All sides agreed we could not cut off power."

Power workers at AO Yakutenergo in the capital of Sakha, or Yakutia, turned off electricity in parts of the Siberian republic for part of last week to protest non-payment of power bills by local companies and the local government.
Local press reports last week said the diamond-mining region in Western Yakutia had not been affected by power cuts.
Lukishin said ARS and Yakutenergo leaders negotiated successfully on September 26 and 27, he said, though he declined to give details of agreements.

Spiridon Sosin, chairman of the Federation of Sakha-Yakutia Trade Unions, said workers had stopped temporary blackouts centered on the capital on Thursday after the local government agreed to pay its energy bill.
"There was no strike. Just temporary power cuts," he said by telephone from Yukutia's capital, Yakutsk.

Lukishin said ARS was not threatened by power cuts over the winter. "We have fuel reserves for the winter. It is impossible to compare us to the Primorye region," Lukishin said, referring to a strike in Russia's Far East Pacific coast region which includes Vladivostok port.
He said ARS and Yakutenergo still disagreed on whether the mine owed money for back energy bills but that ARS was paying all current power bills on time.
